_comment: Which n8n instances exist, and which workflows are worth watching. Tracked on purpose, exactly like checks.example.json: a workflow registered here starts being collected on srv1340120 by itself on the next pull. Nothing in this file is secret — base URLs, workflow ids, node names, an email list. The API KEY is never here: it is read from the environment variable named by apiKeyEnv, server-side only, and never written to data/ or the page.
_instances_comment: The allowlist: a workflow may only name an instance declared here. TWO WAYS TO READ AN N8N. `source: sqlite` reads n8n's own database with a read-only SELECT over SSH — no API key to create or rotate, no public port, no n8n configuration at all, and the same SSH-plus-a-read-only-command idiom every other fact on this dashboard already arrives by (see kw-collect.sh). That is what this estate uses, because the public API is not available here. `source: api` is the REST API and stays for an n8n Cloud instance that has no database to reach; it needs apiKeyEnv and a baseUrl, and registry.js refuses a plain-HTTP baseUrl that is not loopback. publicUrl is only ever used to build clickable links on the dashboard.

n8n-main.note: n8n-n8n-1 on srv1340120. 145 workflows, ~14 active. The dashboard runs on this same box, so the API is reached over LOOPBACK — no DNS, no certificate, no public route, and none of those can break the monitoring by breaking themselves.
n8n-main._why_api_here: The API is the better read for this instance, and measurably so. It hands back jsonSizeBytes with the metadata for free, where SQLite has no stored length and length(d.data) has to read every payload to count it — gigabytes of reading to produce one number per row. It unflattens the execution payload, where reading the table means decoding n8n's flatted encoding first. And a detail fetch is a loopback HTTP request of a few milliseconds rather than a `sqlite3` process spawn. Create the key in n8n: Settings -> n8n API.
n8n-main._sqlite_fallback: To go back to reading the database — no API key, no public port — set source:"sqlite", container:"n8n-n8n-1", dbPath:"/home/node/.n8n/database.sqlite" and drop baseUrl/apiKeyEnv. It needs `apt install -y sqlite3` on the box. Both drivers return identical shapes, so nothing downstream knows which answered.

n8n-vfa2._comment: The SECOND n8n. 3 workflows, 1 active (RxfLvmFe4bAvfxEs, KW META Custom Audiences). Deliberately a DIFFERENT source from n8n-main, and the mix is the point: each instance uses whatever is actually appropriate for how it is reachable. n8n-main is on this box, so loopback HTTP is both fastest and private. This one is on another box with no vhost and no TLS, so an API call would either cross the public internet in clear text — which registry.js refuses — or need a tunnel to be kept alive. Reading its database over SSH needs neither: srv1340120 already holds a key for that box, src/sync.js uses it on every pass, and SSH is the encryption. Set enabled:true once `sqlite3` is installed there and the first pass has been watched.
n8n-vfa2._exposure: Still worth fixing, and now unrelated to this module: the collector found n8n-vfa2-n8n-1 published as 0.0.0.0:32769->5678/tcp — port 32769 on every interface, no vhost, no TLS. ufw being active on that box does NOT cover it, because docker writes its own iptables rules and publishes bypass ufw entirely. Change the compose port mapping to "127.0.0.1:32769:5678" and the exposure goes away without affecting anything local. Reading the database does not need that port at all.

_admin_comment: Who may open the dashboard and the admin panel. Identity comes from Google — an OAuth 2.0 client created in the Google Cloud console — so Estate never sees a password. This list is the authorisation: a valid Google login by an address that is not on it is refused, and the list is re-checked on every request, so removing somebody takes effect immediately rather than when their cookie expires. An EMPTY list denies everyone; a missing config must never be the thing that opens the door. allowedDomain lets anyone at that domain in, which is the convenient option and a much wider one — leave it null unless you mean it. Client id, client secret and session secret are environment variables in /etc/kw-estate.env, never here.
_admin_list_comment: The same seven the daily report already goes to. Kept as named addresses rather than allowedDomain:kwgroup.in on purpose — a domain lets in every account that will ever exist at kwgroup.in, including ones created after whoever set this up has stopped thinking about it, and this page carries every IP, open port and unrotated credential in the estate. Seven names is a list somebody can read and recognise.
_defaults_comment: Applied to every workflow that does not override them. expectedIntervalMin null means 'no schedule expectation' — a webhook-driven workflow is not stale just because nobody filled the form. staleAfterMin null derives as expectedIntervalMin * 2 + 15.
_workflows_comment: Add with: npm run wf-add -- <n8n workflow URL>. The id is parsed out of the URL and checked against the instance before it is written here. `project` must be an id under content/projects/ so the analytics join onto the existing project hierarchy. `checkpoints` are n8n NODE NAMES, spelled exactly as they appear in the editor — they are the stages whose item counts get their own column, which is how you answer 'where did my data disappear'.

_report_comment: The same webhook, recipients and loopback fallback the outside-in check already uses, so there is one mailer to keep working rather than two. The payload carries pre-rendered `html`; the Format report node in deploy/n8n-kw-estate.json passes it straight through when present.

report._notify_comment: The same people the outside-in check already mails, so this works the moment a workflow is connected rather than needing a second list set up. Edit in the admin panel, or here. Both are merged as a union: adding somebody in one place never silently removes the people listed in the other.
report._alerts_comment: Event-driven, not scheduled. cooldownMin is what stops one broken workflow mailing on every pass for a week — the same alert for the same workflow is held for this many minutes after it goes out.

_retention_comment: Two tiers, because raw rows and aggregates have different lifetimes. rawDays/maxRows bound the per-execution table; hourly buckets survive far longer and are what the long-range charts and the baselines read. A workflow running every minute hits maxRows long before rawDays, which is the point: the aggregate keeps the history, the row list stays a readable size.
